summary:
Jakarta stands under Indonesia's national framework, which the national record carries; what is specific to the Special Capital Region is a police practice of raiding private LGBT gatherings under pornography and morality provisions rather than under any Jakarta statute naming LGBT people.

The raid series runs back a decade. In May 2017 police arrested 141 people at what was described as a gay sex party in Jakarta. On 21 May 2017 officers detained 144 people at the Atlantis Gym sauna, ten of whom were charged. In October 2017 police arrested 51 people at a sauna in Central Jakarta, of whom six were charged. All of these cases were pursued under the pornography law.

The pattern continued in 2025. On 1 February 2025 police detained 56 people at a hotel in South Jakarta, described in reporting as a gay party. On 24 May 2025 nine people were detained after a raid on a different hotel in South Jakarta. Offences of this kind can carry up to 15 years' imprisonment.

City government, not only the police, has acted against transgender residents. In March 2018 the Jakarta Social Agency declared transgender waria 'socially dysfunctional' and held trans women in city-run rehabilitation centres unless they signed statements promising not to repeat their offence.

For a trans visitor the operative exposure in Jakarta is attendance at a private gathering: a hotel party, a sauna, a rented venue. The charges that follow are laid under broad pornography and morality provisions with long sentences available, and the sources record no Jakarta statute creating offences specific to LGBT people.
tangentialFactors:
The raid that drew international attention in mid-2025 took place outside the region, at a privately rented villa in the Puncak area near Bogor, where 75 people were arrested. Amnesty International placed the operation inside the Jakarta raid series, said the gathering violated no law, and called the arrests a blatant violation of human rights and privacy. Police made the arrests without naming the detainees or opening judicial proceedings, and those held face up to 15 years under the pornography law. Its deputy director said the raid exemplifies the hostile environment for LGBTI people and demanded the release of those arrested.

Numbers detained in the region have fallen between the two waves: 141, 144 and 51 in the 2017 raids against 56 and nine in the two 2025 South Jakarta hotel raids. These are raw counts of people detained, not rates, and the sources give no figures for how many of those held in 2025 were charged.
localsOnly:
The March 2018 designation of transgender waria as 'socially dysfunctional' was made by the Jakarta Social Agency, a municipal body, and the detention that followed was administrative rather than criminal: trans women were held in city-run rehabilitation centres and released on signing statements promising not to repeat their offence. That is an exposure a short-stay visitor is unlikely to meet, and it shows city institutions, not only the police, acting against transgender people in the region.

For residents the raid series translates into prosecution risk under the pornography and morality provisions: ten of the 144 people detained at the Atlantis Gym sauna in May 2017 and six of the 51 arrested at a Central Jakarta sauna in October 2017 were formally charged, with up to 15 years available on conviction.
outOfScopeNotes:
Charging decisions and outcomes for the 2025 detentions in South Jakarta are not recorded in the sources; only the 2017 raids carry figures for how many of those detained were formally charged. Whether the June 2025 villa detainees near Bogor were charged is likewise not sourced.

No Jakarta-specific data on violence against transgender people appears in the sources consulted, and no Jakarta ordinance or local mechanism on discrimination or hate crime is documented there. Whether the Jakarta Social Agency practice of 2018 continues is not stated.

The December 2022 penal code's entry into force on 2 January 2026 is a national provision; the sources record no Jakarta-specific enforcement data under it, so its practical effect on policing in the capital is unresolved.
